prompt.context: A friend of yours has asked you to invest in his company, which makes dishes for the Mexican market. He has mentioned that he is going to use your investment to purchase a new manufacturing machine that he expects will allow him to double production.
prompt.question: Should you invest in his venture?

clarifying_info.q: How many people live in Mexico?
clarifying_info.a: 110 million people live in Mexico. Assume 100 million for simplicity.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: Population growth can be approximated at 1% per annum.

clarifying_info.q: What is the income distribution in Mexico?
What is the replacement rate for dishes?
Which income segment does the company target?
clarifying_info.a: The company targets the medium segment.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current production capacity?
clarifying_info.a: The company must produce at capacity: 150,000 sets per year. With the new machine, production would double to 300,000 sets per year.

exhibits.title: New Household Dish Sets Demanded per Year (Flow Market)
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down new household formation by income segment, showing population growth, households formed, and the number of dish sets purchased by segment.

framework: 1. Market sizing — estimate total addressable market (stock: replacement demand; flow: new household demand) and identify the relevant segment
2. Competitive landscape — understand who the key competitors are and what market share they hold in the target segment
3. Company capabilities & break-even — assess what the new machine enables, the break-even volume, and whether existing operations provide leverageable cost advantages
4. Investment recommendation — synthesize market feasibility, competitive position, and profitability to advise yes/no and conditions

questions.prompt: Size the total Mexican dish market by replacement demand (the 'stock').
questions.guidance: Divide population by average household size to get households. Multiply by sets per income tier. Apply 15% replacement rate to each tier. Strong candidates clearly segment high/medium/low and sum to a total.

math.setup: Population = 100M. Avg household size = 4. Households = 25M. High (5%) = 1.25M HH x 3 sets = 3.75M sets, replacement = 562,500. Medium (45%) = 11.25M HH x 2 sets = 22.5M sets, replacement = 3,375,000. Low (50%) = 12.5M HH x 1 set = 12.5M sets, replacement = 1,875,000.
math.answer: ~3.4 million sets/year for the medium segment (replacement only).

questions.prompt: Size the new demand from household formation (the 'flow') and combine with the replacement figure to get total medium-segment market size.
questions.guidance: Apply 1% growth to total households to get new HH per year. Allocate by income share, multiply by sets per tier. Note these new HHs also start generating replacement demand in subsequent years, but the immediate effect is the initial purchase.

math.setup: New HH = 25,000,000 x 1% = 250,000. Medium share = 45%. New medium HH = 112,500. Sets purchased = 112,500 x 2 = 225,000. Total medium segment = 3,375,000 + 225,000 = 3,600,000.
steps: New sets bought by medium HH = 112,500 x 2 = 225,000
math.answer: ~3.6 million sets/year total for the medium segment.

questions.prompt: Given that break-even requires producing at full capacity of 150,000 sets/year, and the new machine doubles production to 300,000 sets/year, assess market feasibility.
questions.guidance: Compare post-investment production to total addressable segment. 300,000 / 3,600,000 ≈ 8.3%, which is less than 10% of the medium segment. At first glance the market is large enough. However, raise the caveat that current competitive dynamics matter — if a rival already holds 70%+ share, the remaining accessible market is much smaller.

math.setup: Post-investment capacity = 300,000 sets/year. Medium segment = ~3,600,000 sets/year.
math.answer: 300,000 sets = ~8% of medium segment — market is large enough in absolute terms, pending competitive analysis.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional areas would you explore before finalizing the investment recommendation?

categories.name: Competitive landscape
ideas: Current market share of the friend's company
Identity and share of key competitors
Whether a dominant competitor (e.g., >70% share) limits accessible market
Barriers to entry and differentiation in the segment

categories.name: Company financials & unit economics
ideas: COGS breakdown and how the new machine changes unit cost
Payback period on the machine investment

categories.name: Operational capability
ideas: Ability to scale distribution to sell 300,000 sets
Sales force and retail channel relationships

categories.name: Market trends
ideas: Shifts in consumer preference for dish materials or designs
Risk of substitutes (e.g., disposable or imported dishes)
Trade dynamics and import competition in Mexico
Regulatory or tariff changes affecting inputs

categories.name: Other demand segments
ideas: Restaurants, hotels, offices — additional addressable market not yet quantified
Export potential to other Latin American markets

recommendation: The medium-segment dish market in Mexico is approximately 3.6 million sets per year — large enough to absorb 300,000 sets (about 8% share) at full doubled capacity.
The investment appears feasible from a market-size perspective, but should be conditional on confirming no dominant competitor controls the majority of the segment.
risks: A competitor with 70%+ market share could leave insufficient accessible volume for the company to reach break-even.
Production doubling does not guarantee sales growth — distribution and channel capacity must be validated.
Population and income-distribution assumptions are estimates; actual market size could differ materially.
New household formation (flow demand) is only ~225,000 sets/year for the medium segment, so growth is modest relative to total market.
next_steps: Obtain competitive market share data for the medium-segment dish market.
Conduct detailed break-even and payback analysis on the machine cost.
Validate distribution capacity to sell 300,000 sets annually.
Assess the company's current cost structure to identify leverage points post-investment.
Consider whether other demand segments (restaurants, hotels) could provide additional revenue to improve the investment case.
